advances: An actual convex-body regularity obstruction to identifying faces by differential rank. It does not obstruct repair along the actual generators, whose conditional law here is uniform.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Choose a compact nowhere-dense subset $E\subset(0,1)$ of positive length. For instance, in $[1/4,3/4]$ remove open intervals around a countable dense subset with total length less than $1/2$. Define
$$
g(x)=\int_0^x\mathbf 1_{[0,1]\setminus E}(t)\,dt,\qquad f(x)=\int_0^x g(s)\,ds,\qquad 0\le x\le1.
$$
The function $g$ is Lipschitz and strictly increasing because every nonempty open interval contains an open subinterval off $E$. Thus $f$ is strictly convex and $C^{1,1}$ with derivative $g$ and with $f''=0$ almost everywhere on $E$. Since $0\le g(x)\le x$, one has $0\le f(x)\le1/2$. The body
$$
K=\{(x,y):0\le x\le1,\ f(x)\le y\le2\}\times[0,1]
$$
is compact, convex, and full-dimensional. On its lower cylindrical patch use $X(x,s)=(x,f(x),s)$ and $n(x)=(g(x),-1,0)/\sqrt{1+g(x)^2}$ for $0<x,s<1$. Strict convexity makes the supporting line of the planar epigraph in this direction meet the graph only at $(x,f(x))$. Consequently the corresponding exposed face of $K$ is the full vertical segment at that point, of dimension one.

The original patch has area density $\sqrt{1+g(x)^2}\,dx\,ds$. Its normal map depends only on $x$ and is injective as a function of $x$. Hence $E\times(0,1)$ has positive area, and disintegrating the displayed density along each normal gives uniform $s$ on its generator. Except for edges of surface measure zero, no other patch has normals $n(x)$ with $0<x<1$, because the other planar faces have a coordinate normal different from these directions, since $0<g(x)$ for $x>0$. To see nullity of $n(E)$, the relatively open complement of $E$ in $[0,1]$ is a disjoint countable union of intervals with total length $|[0,1]\setminus E|$. The strictly increasing $g$ maps each interval to an interval of the same length, since $g'=1$ there. The length of $g([0,1])$ is exactly $|[0,1]\setminus E|$, so $g(E)$ is null. The map from $g(x)$ to $n(x)$ is Lipschitz on this bounded range, giving $\mathcal H^1(n(E))=0$.

For the unit parallel body set $U(x,s)=X(x,s)+n(x)$. Its supporting normal at $U(x,s)$ is $n(x)$, and the nearest point of $K$ is $X(x,s)$ by the supporting inequality. In fact, every point on the unit parallel boundary has a unique outer unit normal: if $p$ is the point's nearest point of $K$, the boundary point also belongs to the unit ball centered at $p$ inside the parallel body, which forces the normal to be the radial vector at that point. Nearest-point projection onto $K$ is nonexpansive. Indeed the two projection inequalities imply $\lVert p-q\rVert^2\le(p-q)\cdot(y-w)$ for projections $p,q$ of $y,w$. The coordinate projections of $X$ then show that the inverse of $U$ on its patch is Lipschitz, and $U$ itself is Lipschitz because $g$ is. It carries $E\times(0,1)$ to a set of positive surface area.

At almost every $x\in E$, $g'(x)=0$ and $n'(x)=0$. At every such parameter and every $0<s<1$, the derivative of $U$ has independent columns $(1,g(x),0)$ and $(0,0,1)$. The derivative of $n(x)$ in these parameters is zero, and the bi-Lipschitz inverse makes its tangential derivative on the parallel patch zero. Thus its rank there is zero, and the proposed formula $2-\operatorname{rank}(D\text{Gauss})$ gives two, whereas the original exposed face has dimension one.

statement: There is a full-dimensional compact convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ whose unit parallel body has Gauss map of tangential differential rank zero on a set of positive surface area, although all corresponding exposed faces of $K$ have dimension one. The normals in this example form a set of zero $\mathcal H^1$ measure with positive mass for the original surface-area normal marginal. On the generators with these normals the original conditional surface law is uniform.
title: Parallel-body Gauss rank need not determine exposed-face dimension
